name: Estimation and Prioritisation
one_liner: Relative points and velocity to size the work; MoSCoW to decide what survives.
purpose: Agile estimating incorporates the notion of just enough upfront detail, balancing estimation effort against available information and the accuracy needed. PM²-Agile estimation rests on three concepts — Relative Estimate, Velocity and Absolute Estimate — because humans are better at making relative estimations. Work Items are then prioritised according to delivery value and contribution to project goals, with techniques such as MoSCoW enabling contingency management.
meta: 60% Must have, 20% Should have, 20% Could have

items: Relative Estimate — high-level size of a work item, typically measured in points
Velocity — the number of points the A-PCT can deliver within an iteration
Absolute Estimate — translates the size in points into effort, typically in Actual Hours
Must have — the minimum usable subset that must be delivered
Should have — important but not vital this time
Could have — desirable if capacity allows
Won't have this time — explicitly excluded from this delivery
Suggested effort split: 60% Must, 20% Should, 20% Could
Humans are better at making relative estimations than absolute ones
Points size work items in relation to other work items, not in person-days
Relative estimates get more accurate as problem and solution become clearer
Planning Poker is the recommended relative-estimation technique
Priority is negotiated against the team's estimates
MoSCoW empowers the team to define the minimum usable subset or MVP
When Should and Could items cannot be tackled in time, contingency is applied
What ships is still the agreed most relevant features — the Must haves

fields.what: Agile estimating balances estimation effort against the information available and the accuracy expected of the estimate.
fields.pollux: The team sizes the next items, not all 1,850 person-days upfront.

fields.what: A high-level estimate of a work item's size, typically measured using a neutral unit such as points.
fields.pollux: Items are sized against each other, not in Levallois Systems day rates.

fields.what: Measures the number of points the Agile Project Core Team can deliver within an iteration.
fields.pollux: Measured per two-week iteration and reported to you by Lovelace.

fields.what: Translates a work item's size in points into an objective, detailed estimate of effort, typically in Actual Hours.
fields.pollux: Used where the seconded contract needs hours rather than points.

fields.what: Relative estimates rest on the fact that humans are better at making relative estimations than absolute ones.
fields.pollux: Lamarr compares a new view to one already built rather than guessing hours.

fields.what: Relative estimates tend to become more accurate as the project progresses and problem and solution become clearer.
fields.pollux: Estimates in Release 3 are better than those in iteration 1.

fields.what: Team velocity is important to track for planning regular iterations and for measuring team performance.
fields.pollux: Feeds the Development Status Report and the four release dates.

fields.what: The guide points to Planning Poker as the point-based relative estimating technique, detailed in the Tools and Techniques publication.
fields.pollux: Used in refinement sessions Curie shares in advance.

fields.what: Work Items are prioritised according to their delivery value and their contribution toward achieving project goals.
fields.pollux: Items serving criteria SC1 to SC5 outrank convenience features.

fields.what: Agreeing and negotiating each work item's priority, considering the team's estimates, enables contingency management for the project.
fields.pollux: Curie negotiates Release 2 content against what the team can size.

fields.what: Must have, Should have, Could have and Won't have this time; it empowers the team to decide collaboratively what the minimum usable subset is.
fields.pollux: Read-only exposure is a Must; the scenario overlay is not, in Release 1.

fields.what: Some methodologies suggest assigning 60% of total effort to Must have, 20% to Should have and 20% to Could have requirements.
fields.pollux: Leaves 40% of each release's effort as usable contingency.

fields.what: When Should and Could items cannot be tackled in the time frame, contingency is applied by still delivering the agreed Must have requirements.
fields.pollux: A slipping release still ships the exposure view the Board needs.

fields.what: Both estimating and prioritising should happen continuously throughout the project so the plan adapts as it progresses.
fields.pollux: Refinement and prioritisation recur inside every two-week iteration.

traps: The suggested MoSCoW split is 60% Must, 20% Should, 20% Could — Won't gets none.
Velocity counts points per iteration; only Absolute Estimates use Actual Hours.
Contingency comes from dropping Should and Could items, not from adding time.
Estimating and prioritising are continuous, not a single upfront exercise.
The glossary spells the W as 'Want to have (but won't have this time)'.
